title: Dodgers looking into Edwin Díaz’s decreased early-season velocity, say closer is not hurt
content:
LOS ANGELES — The Los Angeles Dodgers are trying to suss out why their new closer has seen a notable dip in his velocity. Edwin Díaz and the organization both insist the three-time All-Star is not hurt, even as they try to figure out what is off with him.

Díaz is averaging 95.8 mph on his fastball through the first six appearances of his new three-year, $69 million deal with the Dodgers. That is down from the 97.2 mph he averaged a season ago with the New York Mets, enough for manager Dave Roberts to stay away from Díaz on the second day of a potential back-to-back this weekend against the Texas Rangers. Díaz’s drop in velocity is enough to prompt at least some concern about the health of the reigning back-to-back champions’ new closer.

“Everything I hear, (he says) that he feels fine,” Roberts said Sunday morning. “I think for me, you hear it, you want to completely trust it. But then you’re also looking at the (radar) gun and making sure.

“We’re sort of trying to dig in a little bit. But I think that, you know, two miles an hour, that’s pretty significant.”

That concern level is not high enough for the organization to consider moving Díaz to the injured list, Roberts said. Díaz said Sunday morning he is “feeling really good,” brushing off his diminished velocity due to it being early in the season. Through Díaz’s first six outings, he’s allowed four runs, good for a 6.00 ERA to go with 10 strikeouts and four saves.

The Dodgers’ bullpen has seemingly fallen into place, knowing Díaz and Timmy Trumpet’s “Narco” are waiting in the ninth inning. Now, they have to sort out why Díaz is still waiting for his velocity to creep up.

Díaz pointed to what he feels has been a trend in recent seasons. For whatever reason, Díaz said, it has taken him time to get his velocity going ever since he tore the patellar tendon in his right knee during the 2023 World Baseball Classic. In the two seasons since, he has seen an uptick from his April radar gun readings as the season has progressed.

“As soon as the season starts going, I start feeling better and better and better,” Díaz said. “And my velo at the end of the year will be what I’m throwing always.”

Díaz’s fastball is still down from where it was last April, from 96.3 mph to 95.8 mph. The right-hander averaged 95.5 mph with the pitch on Friday, when he suffered his first blown save as a Dodger and surrendered three runs against the Rangers. He cleared 95.8 mph just three times over the 23-pitch outing.

“I was feeling good,” Díaz said. “But I didn’t have my best stuff that day.”

That prompted the Dodgers to make Díaz unavailable for Saturday’s 6-3 win over Texas, with Blake Treinen and Alex Vesia combining to record the final three outs. While Díaz said Sunday morning he felt he could be available to pitch, Roberts said the team will “yellow light” him and take his availability on a day-by-day basis while it sorts out what is going on.

Roberts said he did not believe Díaz’s mechanics are causing his delivery to drop. When asked about the possibility that Díaz might be pitching through a physical issue that he hasn’t disclosed, Roberts said the club’s pitching coaches have stressed to Díaz to be honest about how he’s feeling.

“Players want to play,” Roberts said. “They want to perform. Sometimes they’re their worst enemy. I think that’s another reason why we’re kind of just, again, treading lightly is the word I’m using. Because you’ve got to respect that they want to be out there. But then we all kind of end up with the short straw if the player goes down.”

The Dodgers still have the luxury of not pushing Díaz. They acquired him to help them win in October, not get them there. Their bullpen has been a bright spot in the early going, producing a 3.60 ERA. Three of the 18 runs the group has allowed this season came in Díaz’s blown save.

Still, Díaz is an important figure. The group’s stability is predicated in part on Díaz’s presence, which fits each member into a role. Roberts can use pitchers such as Vesia and Treinen in high-leverage spots, knowing he doesn’t have to worry about them being available for the ninth. Tanner Scott, the team’s closer for much of last season, has had a promising start to the season in part because the Dodgers have been able to deploy him in favorable matchups in different parts of the game.

Scott represented a rare splurge from the organization on a free-agent reliever. His massive struggles in 2025 (the first year of a four-year, $72 million deal) underscored the risk in spending at the position. The Dodgers doubled down with Díaz anyway, banking on one of the most accomplished closers in the sport to help solve their bullpen issues.

Now, they have to figure out what’s going on with him.
